subject: History
source: Edexcel GCSE History 1HI0 Paper 3 modern depth study option 32: Weimar and Nazi Germany, 1918-39 (Key Topic 2: Hitler's rise to power, 1919-33, plus the start of Key Topic 3). Option set chosen for the school: Paper 1 Crime and punishment in Britain c1000-present with Whitechapel (taught in Y10); Paper 2 Superpower relations and the Cold War 1941-91 with Early Elizabethan England 1558-88; Paper 3 Weimar and Nazi Germany. No school Drive history material for this option, written from the specification and subject knowledge

lessons.title: The early Nazi Party, 1919-22
objectives: Describe how the German Workers' Party became the Nazi Party
Explain the main ideas of the Nazi 25-point programme and the role of the SA

keywords.def: National Socialist German Workers' Party, led by Hitler from 1921
the Nazi policy statement of 1920
Sturmabteilung, the Nazi paramilitary 'stormtroopers'
a person or group unfairly blamed for problems
the 1919 peace treaty that Germany was forced to accept

starter: Name two terms of the Treaty of Versailles.
What was hyperinflation and when did it occur?
Who was the first President of the Weimar Republic?

teach.heading: Bismillah: understanding how extremism grows
bullets: We study the Nazis to prevent hatred happening again
Hitler joined a small party in 1919
Weimar Germany faced political and economic crisis
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Emphasise that we study this period to understand how prejudice can be spread and how to resist it. Check retrieval: Weimar problems (Versailles, hyperinflation, instability, the Spartacists and Kapp Putsch).

teach.heading: From DAP to NSDAP
bullets: Hitler joined the German Workers' Party in 1919
It was renamed the Nazi Party in 1920
Hitler became leader in July 1921
teach.note: Hitler was an army intelligence agent sent to watch the party. He became its main speaker. By 1921 he had pushed out Anton Drexler. Ask why Hitler's speaking style attracted people.

teach.heading: The 25-point programme
bullets: Cancel the Treaty of Versailles
Unite all German-speaking peoples
Remove Jews' rights as citizens
teach.note: Announced in February 1920. Handle antisemitism factually and with sensitivity: the Nazis used Jews as scapegoats. Include also: land reform and anti-capitalist ideas which appealed to workers. Ask who might support such ideas and why.

teach.heading: The SA
bullets: Founded 1921 as the party's protection force
Brown-shirted stormtroopers attacked opponents
Ernst Röhm later became a leader
teach.note: SA men guarded meetings and intimidated enemies. Violence was part of the Nazi strategy. By 1923 the Nazis had around 55,000 members. Use 'about' for membership.

practice: When did the party become the Nazi Party?
Name two aims of the 25-point programme.
What was the job of the SA?
independent: Create a timeline of 1919-22 with five events
Explain two reasons why Nazi ideas appealed to some Germans in the early 1920s
Write: Why was Hitler an effective leader of the early Nazi Party? (paragraph)
lessons.homework: Write a short note on how the 25-point programme used the grievances of Versailles.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: timeline cards and a key terms mat. Stretch: evaluate whether Nazi propaganda was more about ideas or about fear.

lessons.title: The Munich Putsch and Mein Kampf, 1923-24
objectives: Explain the causes, events and consequences of the Munich Putsch
Describe what Hitler learned from its failure

keywords.def: an attempted violent takeover of government
French and Belgian seizure of the Ruhr in January 1923
'My Struggle', Hitler's book written in prison in 1924
betraying one's country by trying to overthrow its government
living space: Hitler's idea of land for Germans in eastern Europe

starter: Define hyperinflation.
Why did France occupy the Ruhr?
Name the Nazi Party leader.

teach.heading: Crisis in 1923
bullets: France occupied the Ruhr in January 1923
Hyperinflation destroyed savings
Many Germans lost faith in Weimar
teach.note: Recap: Germany missed reparations; the government printed money; Stresemann called off passive resistance in September and introduced the Rentenmark in November. Ask why this was a good moment for extremists.

teach.heading: The Beer Hall Putsch, 8-9 November 1923
bullets: Hitler and the SA seized a Munich beer hall
He hoped to march on Berlin like Mussolini's March on Rome
Police opened fire the next day; 16 Nazis died
teach.note: Mention General Ludendorff's support and the kidnapped Bavarian leaders. The putsch failed because the Bavarian authorities did not support Hitler and the police acted. Use the figure 16 Nazi marchers killed plus 4 police.

teach.heading: Trial and prison
bullets: Hitler was tried for treason in 1924
He used the trial to publicise his ideas
He served about nine months of a five-year sentence
teach.note: The judges were sympathetic, which tells us about attitudes in Bavaria. He was sentenced to five years and released in December 1924. Ask pupils what a trial can do for a leader's public image.

teach.heading: Mein Kampf and new tactics
bullets: He wrote Mein Kampf in prison
It set out his ideas: racism, Lebensraum, hatred of communism
He decided to win power by elections, not force
teach.note: Mein Kampf was published in 1925-26. Stress that these ideas were openly stated. Ask pupils how an organisation can change tactics while keeping its goals. Handle with care and offer firm moral framing.

practice: Why did the Munich Putsch fail?
What did Hitler do in prison?
What was the main lesson Hitler learned?
independent: Write a narrative account of the Munich Putsch in six sentences
Explain two consequences of the putsch for the Nazi Party
Answer: Was the Munich Putsch a failure or a success for Hitler?
lessons.homework: Complete a cause and consequence chart for the Munich Putsch.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequence cards for the putsch narrative. Stretch: judge which of Hitler's tactics mattered more: force or propaganda.

lessons.title: The lean years, 1924-29
objectives: Explain why the Nazis had little success between 1924 and 1929
Describe how the party reorganised under Hitler

keywords.def: German leader who restored economic stability in the 1920s
the 1924 plan reducing reparations payments and giving US loans
a 1926 meeting where Hitler reasserted control of the party
a regional party leader
the Nazi organisation for young people

starter: Why was the Munich Putsch important?
What is Mein Kampf?
Name one reason why Germany recovered in the mid-1920s.

teach.heading: A recovering Germany
bullets: The Dawes Plan (1924) brought US loans
The Locarno Treaties (1925) improved relations
Germany joined the League of Nations in 1926
teach.note: Link to Stresemann's achievements. Ask why extremist parties do badly when people have jobs and hope. In 1928 the Nazis won only 12 seats (2.6% of the vote).

teach.heading: Rebuilding the party
bullets: The ban on the Nazis was lifted in 1925
At Bamberg in 1926 Hitler gained control over rivals
Regional leaders, Gauleiters, were appointed
teach.note: At Bamberg, Hitler asserted the Führerprinzip over those like Gregor Strasser who wanted a more socialist focus. Ask why unity and loyalty to one leader helped the party.

teach.heading: Organisation and young people
bullets: The SS formed under Himmler in 1929 as an elite
The Hitler Youth recruited young people
Membership grew to about 108,000 by 1928
teach.note: Membership figures are approximate. Highlight how the party built structures and a network while it was weak in elections. Link to long-term planning.

teach.heading: Why limited support?
bullets: Most Germans were doing better
Moderate parties held the middle ground
The party was seen as a fringe
teach.note: Ask pupils: if the Depression had not happened, would Hitler have come to power? Use as a bridge to the next lesson on contingency.

practice: Name two reasons the Nazis were unpopular 1924-29.
What happened at Bamberg?
How many seats did the Nazis win in 1928?
independent: Create a table: Nazi strengths vs weaknesses in 1928
Write an answer: Explain why the Nazis did not do well in elections 1924-29
Plan a response to: 'Hitler's rise was inevitable.' How far do you agree?
exit: Give one reason the Nazis had little support in 1928.
Name one way the Nazis were preparing for the future.
lessons.homework: Draw a graph or table of Nazi Reichstag seats 1924-1932 from data supplied in class.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: simplified data table and cause sort. Stretch: assess the claim that the lean years were important for the later Nazi success.

lessons.title: The Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression in Germany
objectives: Explain how the Wall Street Crash affected Germany
Describe the political consequences of the Depression, including Nazi gains

keywords.def: the collapse of the US stock market in October 1929
a severe, long fall in economic activity with high unemployment
when people who want to work cannot find jobs
the head of the German government
a law letting the President rule by emergency decree

starter: What was the Dawes Plan?
How many seats did the Nazis win in 1928?
What did US loans do for Germany?

teach.heading: Crash in New York
bullets: The US stock market collapsed in October 1929
US banks recalled their loans to Germany
German businesses closed
teach.note: Explain why dependence on US loans made Germany vulnerable. Ask pupils to trace the chain of cause: crash, loans recalled, factories close, unemployment.

teach.heading: Unemployment
bullets: Unemployment rose from about 1.4 million in 1929
It reached around 6 million by 1932
Middle-class savings and farms suffered
teach.note: Use approximate figures. Include human impact: families struggling, soup kitchens, young men without work. Many looked for someone to blame.

teach.heading: Politics in crisis
bullets: Chancellor Brüning cut spending and raised taxes
Governments ruled by Article 48 decrees
Support moved to extremist parties
teach.note: Brüning's policy made things worse for many. Parliament lost power. Ask: how can a democracy be damaged by its own emergency laws?

teach.heading: Nazi gains
bullets: 1928: 12 seats and 2.6% of the vote
July 1932: 230 seats and 37.3%
teach.note: Use the data to draw a graph. The Communist Party also grew, which frightened the middle class and business leaders. Ask pupils why Nazi propaganda promised 'work and bread'.

practice: Why did the Crash affect Germany so badly?
How did unemployment change between 1929 and 1932?
What happened to the Nazi vote between 1928 and 1932?
independent: Make a flow chart from the Crash to the rise in Nazi votes
Write a paragraph: Explain why the Depression helped the Nazis
Evaluate: How far was the Depression the main reason for Hitler's rise?
exit: Name the economic event of October 1929.
Give the Nazis' seats in July 1932.
lessons.homework: Write a 12-mark style answer: Explain why the Great Depression helped Hitler's rise.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: flow-chart pieces to arrange. Stretch: compare the effects of the Depression on workers and the middle class.

lessons.title: Why did people vote Nazi? Propaganda, the SA and Hitler's appeal
objectives: Explain the methods the Nazis used to win support
Assess why different groups voted Nazi in 1930-32

keywords.def: information, often biased, used to promote a cause
the Nazi propaganda chief from 1930
a large public meeting to show support
a medium for mass communication at that time
the quality that attracts people

starter: How many seats did the Nazis win in 1930?
What was Article 48?
Why did people turn to extremist parties?

teach.heading: Hitler's message
bullets: He blamed Versailles, the Jews and communists
He promised jobs, order and national pride
He promised to make Germany strong again
teach.note: Emphasise that hatred was used to gain votes, and that it is our duty to challenge such lies. Pupils should recognise how simple messages can be attractive in a crisis.

teach.heading: Propaganda methods
bullets: Goebbels organised posters, newspapers and films
Rallies had flags, uniforms and torchlight
Hitler flew to many cities in 1932
teach.note: In 1932 Hitler's 'Germany Flight' campaign was a new technique. Show example posters; ask pupils to analyse their messages for different audiences (farmers, workers, women).

teach.heading: Targeting groups
bullets: Farmers: higher prices and protection
Workers: jobs and order
Middle class and business: stop communism
teach.note: Ask why different groups were drawn to different promises, even if these conflicted. The Nazis were catch-all but especially strong among Protestants, small towns and the middle classes.

teach.heading: Violence and intimidation
bullets: The SA fought communists in the streets
Fear made some voters want order
Violence made democracy seem weak
teach.note: By 1932 the SA had about 400,000 members. Link to political instability: voters saw the government as unable to stop street fighting. Avoid suggesting the Nazis were popular with everyone: nearly two-thirds never voted for them.

practice: Name two propaganda methods used by the Nazis.
Which groups did Nazi policies target?
Why did violence help the Nazis?
independent: Analyse a Nazi election poster: message, audience, technique
Write a PEEL paragraph: Explain why the Nazis won support in 1930-32
Rank the five most important reasons for Nazi success and justify your top two
exit: Name one group that voted Nazi and why.
lessons.homework: Design a poster that critiques Nazi propaganda techniques, using what you have learned.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: poster analysis frame. Stretch: evaluate the reliability of a Nazi election poster as evidence of why people voted Nazi.

lessons.title: Political intrigue, 1932-33: Hindenburg, Papen and Schleicher
objectives: Explain why Hindenburg agreed to appoint Hitler as Chancellor

keywords.def: President of Germany 1925-34
Franz von Papen, Chancellor June to November 1932
General Kurt von Schleicher, Chancellor December 1932 to January 1933
a government made up of more than one party
secret plotting for political advantage

starter: How many seats did the Nazis win in July 1932?
What was Article 48?
Name the Chancellor who followed Brüning.

teach.heading: Presidential election, 1932
bullets: Hindenburg beat Hitler in 1932
Hitler won 13.4 million votes in the run-off
He proved he had mass support
teach.note: The run-off was in April 1932: Hindenburg about 19.4 million votes, Hitler about 13.4 million. Use approximations. Ask whether losing weakened Hitler or strengthened his claim to be a national figure.

teach.heading: Papen and the Reichstag
bullets: Papen became Chancellor in June 1932
He lifted the ban on the SA
July 1932: Nazis became the largest party
teach.note: Hitler demanded to be Chancellor; Hindenburg refused, calling Hitler a 'Bohemian corporal'. Ask pupils why the Nazis were not given power despite being the largest party.

teach.heading: November 1932 election
bullets: Nazi seats fell to 196
The Nazi vote dropped to 33.1%
The party had money problems
teach.note: Highlight: the Nazis' peak may have passed. Ask pupils whether this makes Hitler's appointment in January surprising. Introduce the idea of 'contingency': chance events and individual decisions.

teach.heading: The backroom deal
bullets: Schleicher failed to build a majority
Papen made a deal with Hitler
Papen believed he could 'control' him
teach.note: Papen persuaded Hindenburg that conservatives in the cabinet would contain Hitler: only three Nazis in a cabinet of 11. Ask: what did the conservatives misjudge? This is a key lesson about miscalculation.

practice: Why did Hindenburg refuse to appoint Hitler in 1932?
What happened in the November 1932 election?
Why did Papen think he could control Hitler?
independent: Create a timeline from March 1932 to January 1933
Explain why Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933 using three causes
Answer: Was Hitler's appointment mainly due to Nazi strength or other people's mistakes?
exit: Give one mistake made by Papen.
lessons.homework: Write a 16-mark style judgement paragraph on Hitler's appointment: was it inevitable?
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: character cards for Hindenburg, Papen, Schleicher. Stretch: evaluate the role of individuals compared with economic conditions.

lessons.title: Hitler becomes Chancellor, January 1933
objectives: Describe the events of 30 January 1933 and its immediate aftermath
Evaluate the reasons for Hitler's success in gaining power

keywords.def: the head of the German government
the group of senior ministers in a government
the German parliament
relating to a system in which people vote for their government
to make power stronger and more secure

starter: Who advised Hindenburg to appoint Hitler?
How many Nazi ministers were in the cabinet?
Name one Nazi propaganda method.

teach.heading: 30 January 1933
bullets: Hindenburg appointed Hitler as Chancellor
The Nazis held three of 11 cabinet posts
Torchlit parades celebrated in Berlin
teach.note: Use a photograph. Note: Hitler came to power legally, not by a coup. Ask pupils why that matters. Hermann Göring became Interior Minister of Prussia, controlling the police.

teach.heading: A shaky coalition?
bullets: Hitler's party did not have a majority
Hitler asked for a new election
He wanted more power for the Nazis
teach.note: Hitler used the Chancellor's post to call a new election for 5 March 1933. Ask: how could he use state resources, such as radio and police, in the campaign?

teach.heading: Why Hitler succeeded
bullets: Long-term: Versailles, instability, weak Weimar
Medium-term: the Depression and Nazi organisation
Short-term: the 1932-33 political deals
teach.note: Ask pupils to build a causal diagram with these three levels and then rank. Link to the historical skill of separating long-term from short-term causes. Emphasise multiple causation.

teach.heading: Warning signs
bullets: Weimar democracy had few committed defenders
Many elites underestimated Hitler
Violence and hatred had been normalised
teach.note: Link to personal responsibility and standing up against prejudice. Encourage pupils to discuss, respectfully, why people stay silent and how communities can resist hatred.

practice: Explain how Hitler became Chancellor legally.
Why did conservatives agree to the deal?
Name two long-term causes of Nazi success.
independent: Make a diagram of long-term, medium-term and short-term causes of Hitler's rise
Write an answer: Explain why Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933 (12 marks)
Rank causes and justify your top choice
exit: On which date did Hitler become Chancellor?
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark explanation and exchange with a partner to peer-mark.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: causal diagram with pre-written cards. Stretch: argue which cause was the 'trigger' and which a 'necessary condition'.

lessons.title: The Reichstag Fire and the Enabling Act, 1933
objectives: Explain how the Reichstag Fire helped Hitler remove democratic limits
Describe the Enabling Act of March 1933 and its consequences

keywords.def: the fire that damaged the German parliament building on 27 February 1933

keywords.term: Decree for the Protection of the People and State
keywords.def: an emergency law of 28 February 1933 that removed civil liberties
the March 1933 law letting Hitler's government make laws without the Reichstag
rule by one person or party with unlimited power
freedoms such as free speech and protection from arrest

starter: What does 'consolidate' mean?
When did Hitler become Chancellor?
Name the German parliament.

teach.heading: The fire
bullets: On 27 February 1933 the Reichstag burned
A Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, was arrested
Historians still debate who started the fire
teach.note: Present both views: some say van der Lubbe acted alone; others, at the time, suspected the Nazis. State clearly that the evidence is debated, but that the Nazis used the fire to claim a communist plot.

teach.heading: Emergency decree
bullets: 28 February: the decree removed freedom of speech
It allowed arrest without trial
Communists were arrested in thousands
teach.note: Ask: how does an emergency law change a democracy? Use of fear to justify the removal of rights is an important lesson. Link to the importance of justice and rights.

teach.heading: March 1933 election
bullets: The Nazis won 43.9% of the vote
They still had no majority alone
The SA intimidated voters
teach.note: Ask pupils why even with violence and propaganda the Nazis only reached 43.9%. They needed the Nationalists' support for a majority.

teach.heading: The Enabling Act, 23 March
bullets: It passed by 444 votes to 94
Only the Social Democrats voted against
Hitler could make laws without the Reichstag for four years
teach.note: The Communists had been arrested or banned, and Social Democrat deputies were intimidated; the Catholic Centre Party voted in favour after promises. This marked the end of democracy in Germany. It leads into Key Topic 3: Nazi control and dictatorship.

practice: What did the Decree of 28 February do?
How did the Nazis use the Reichstag Fire?
Why was the Enabling Act important?
independent: Write a narrative of the events from 27 February to 23 March 1933
Explain two ways the Nazis turned a legal appointment into a dictatorship
Answer: How far did the Reichstag Fire help Hitler gain power? (16-mark style)
exit: Give one consequence of the Enabling Act.
lessons.homework: Prepare a revision mat for Key Topic 2 (Hitler's rise to power) with 12 key dates.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequence cards for the narrative. Stretch: assess whether the Enabling Act was a turning point or the result of earlier decisions.
